大学の英語の発表、お題自由だったので迷わず自分のアプリ「FesRegi」の話にしますｗ
ユーザー785人、登録模擬店262店、注文19,700件、iOSは1週間で200DL数字にすると改めてすごいなと実感
英語頑張ります💪

Hello, everyone. Today, I want to talk about something I made. It is called "FesRegi." FesRegi is a free app for school festivals. It helps students sell food and drinks easily. I made this app by myself.

In high school, I worked at a food stall at my school festival. We used paper to write orders. It was slow, and we often made mistakes. So, I thought, "I will make my own app." Now, with FesRegi, students can use a computer or a smartphone as a cash register. Customers can also order from their phone with a QR code. No more long lines!

Now, FesRegi is used in many schools. Let me show you some numbers. More than 785 people use FesRegi now. More than 260 shops are registered. And students have made about 19,700 orders with this app! I am very happy about these numbers.

There is more good news. On June 29, I released an iOS app for FesRegi. It is very new, only about one week old. But already, more than 200 people downloaded it! I think many more people will use it in the future.

In conclusion, FesRegi is a free, easy, and useful app for school festivals. It helps students sell things without stress. If your school has a festival, please try FesRegi. Thank you for listening!

日本語翻訳

皆さん、こんにちは。今日は私が作ったものについて話したいと思います。それは「FesRegi」というものです。FesRegiは学校の文化祭のための無料アプリです。生徒が食べ物や飲み物を簡単に売るのを助けます。私はこのアプリを一人で作りました。 

私が高校生のとき、文化祭の模擬店で働いていました。私たちは紙に注文を書いていました。遅くて、よく間違えていました。それで、「自分でアプリを作ろう」と思いました。今、FesRegiを使えば、生徒はパソコンやスマートフォンをレジとして使えます。お客さんもQRコードを使って自分のスマホから注文できます。もう長い行列はありません！

 今、FesRegiは多くの学校で使われています。いくつかの数字を紹介します。現在、785人以上がFesRegiを使っています。260店舗以上が登録されています。そして、生徒たちはこのアプリで約19,700件の注文をしました！私はこの数字にとても満足しています。

 もっと良いニュースがあります。6月29日に、FesRegiのiOSアプリをリリースしました。とても新しく、まだ1週間ほどです。しかし、すでに200人以上がダウンロードしてくれました！これからもっと多くの人が使ってくれると思います。 

結論として、FesRegiは無料で、簡単で、学校の文化祭に役立つアプリです。生徒がストレスなく物を売るのを助けます。もしあなたの学校に文化祭があれば、ぜひFesRegiを試してみてください。聞いてくれてありがとうございました！

Google AI Studio just landed on iPhone — and the App Store listing reveals something interesting.

114 MB binary. iOS 18+. 76 languages. Released July 1, 2026.

This isn't just a mobile port of the web interface. At 114 MB for a cloud-first product, they're bundling meaningful local modules — likely on-device prompt processing, offline caching, and local inference for small models.

The bigger story: Google is making a direct play for the "vibe coding" workflow on mobile. The tagline is "build your ideas wherever inspiration strikes" — which translates to: you can prototype, test prompts, and iterate on AI apps from your phone without touching a laptop.

Competitive positioning matters here:
- OpenAI has the ChatGPT app (chat-first, not build-first)
- Anthropic has Claude on mobile (conversation, not prototyping)
- Google AI Studio Mobile is build-first — it's Gemini's API playground in your pocket

For developers who prototype on the go — this changes the mobile workflow significantly. Pre-order is live, full launch is here.

data.text: Here’s a quick example with my own experience. Years ago I bought Capcom’s Dead Rising for iOS for $10. Over time Apple released new iOS versions and eventually Capcom would no longer support the game. The iOS game was removed from the App Store and I no longer had access to that game that I bought. Now there are other better examples with the Xbox 360 and PS3 digital titles.

The most underrated desk upgrade of the year is free. It uses the iPad you already own.

A guy on GitHub released OpenSidecar. Free. Open source. peetzweg/opensidecar. You install it on a Mac and any spare Apple device becomes a full second monitor. An old iPad. An iPhone. A second MacBook.

Not a mirror. A real extension of your desktop. You drag a browser window from the Mac straight onto the iPad, scroll with your finger, move around the page like the tablet is a monitor you can hold.

Until this week, that feature cost $100. Duet Display. Luna Display. Apple's own Sidecar with a locked list of supported devices. Three paid products doing what one open source repo now does over Wi-Fi or USB with macOS 14 and iOS 17.

The real idea in the post is not the app.

The real idea is that half the people watching have an iPad in a drawer that became a YouTube player, then a coaster, then dust. It has an M1 chip and a retina display and it is sitting three feet from a laptop that would kill for the extra screen.

Do not buy a second monitor. You already have one. You forgot about it.

The demo is a live prototype. Latency under video editing and games has not been tested. But for a browser window, a Notion doc, a Slack, a spreadsheet, it just works.

The best desk upgrade of the year is not a new display. It is the device you already stopped using.

Max shipped almost 40 iOS apps that make a combined $36,000 a month. He built most of them after work, around a 9-to-5.

On camera he builds a new one, a stamp identifier, in under 20 minutes.

He starts in an ASO tool, not a code editor. His logic: 75% of App Store downloads start with a search, so the keyword is the problem people pay to solve. He types "stamp identifier", filters out crowded terms, checks the competitors, and finds only 4 apps ranked above 100, all released in 2025. Young niche, weak defenders. Keyword locked.

Then the part that took years to earn: his boilerplate. Onboarding, paywall, payments, settings, all prebuilt from 40 previous apps. On top of it he sends Claude Code a 2-sentence prompt: build the camera, gallery, identification, collection and history screens, make it compile. He waits. The app runs.

His money mechanics stay identical across the portfolio. Weekly subscription with a free trial plus a yearly, and a lifetime price for single-use apps. The review prompt fires at the aha moment, right after a successful scan, and never after a failed one.

Visuals take minutes: Gemini draws the icon, competitor screenshots feed the layout, the keyword goes into the title, subtitle and a stuffed 100-character list. Submit.

His advice cuts through the whole genre: thousands of AI apps flood the store every week, so make sure your AI slop beats theirs.

An app a week, after work. The keyword does the marketing.

Hello and welcome to Eye on AI. In today’s edition…Rabbit launches Teach mode for the R1; Microsoft and HarperCollins strike a deal for training data; Google gives Gemini memory; an AI pioneer cites OpenAI’s upcoming model when urging for regulation; Stanford ranks countries on how vibrant their AI ecosystems are. 

Rabbit, maker of the handheld orange AI-in-box device known as the R1, today released a new capability called Teach mode. The mode allows users to “teach” their devices how to perform specific actions by describing the process step-by-step on a computer using natural language and then syncing the lessons to their R1. 

The new capability is a step toward Rabbit’s vision of an app store for model actions—and ultimately, an entirely new way of interacting with devices sans the graphical user interfaces to which we’ve become accustomed. It’s also the latest release from a company that has largely been building its product in public (and Teach mode will be no exception). Critics blasted the R1 at launch as clunky, basically useless, and more of a prototype than a finished product. In conversation with founder and CEO Jesse Lyu ahead of the Teach mode announcement, he described how the company has been using the criticism and user feedback to improve the product, pushing over 20 updates including a second generation of its LAM (large action model) system that makes it possible to interact with any site rather than just the four services available at launch. He framed this back-and-forth as essential, purporting that the only way to build in the AI era is to put a product out in the world and iterate from there. 

An app store for actions

If you watch any of the demo videos for Teach mode, you may think it looks like the most tedious way possible to do something. Take one example where an early tester teaches the device how to draft a tweet. On his computer, he instructs the program to “click the icon to open the box to compose a tweet,” “click inside the text box to start typing,” “type your text inside the box,” and so on before syncing the lesson to the R1.

No coding is required, but it’s still far more involved than just drafting a post on a smartphone or laptop as we always have. Rabbit’s idea, however, is that eventually most users won’t be doing any of this tedious work or interacting with Teach mode at all. Rather than teaching the R1 actions themselves, they will be able to go into an app store of sorts and buy actions created by others. (That’s a bit ironic seeing as Rabbit talks about doing away with apps.)

The store isn’t launching with Teach mode today, however, and Lyu said there’s no timeline for it as they still need to figure out how it will be monetized (both for the company and users who create the actions)to make money from it. For now, users will have access to a limited number of lessons created by early Teach mode testers or be able to create their own. 

“You can imagine, like you train an agent, you should be able to choose whether you want to keep it public or you keep it private. And if you choose to publish it to the public community, and then if a million others are using your license, you should get paid. You should be able to benefit from it, right?” Lyu siad. “So I think this is, to us, the app store for iOS, but for agents.”

The “experimental” disclaimer

The press release announcing Teach mode states that it’s still “experimental” and that “output can be unpredictable.” This is becoming a common disclaimer with the launch of generative AI products. Anthropic, for example, said the same last month when it released Computer Use, which enables its model to use computers the way people do.

Lyu believes this is intrinsic to the nature of how AI works (models aren’t pre-programmed, so you’ll never know exactly what they’ll do) and a result of how fast the technology is developing. 

“You have to kind of encounter all the edge cases and tweak on a fly and continue. That’s just the whole nature of developing with AI models,” he said. In the case of Rabbit in particular, he also also pointed to how the startup doesn’t have a 10-year runway or the resources of a tech giant that would enable it to take its time. “We have to make sure that we take our shot and move fast. This is the only way that we can stay in competition.”

This isn’t to say Rabbit isn’t testing or taking care of issues before launch. The company collaborated with 20 testers to create more than 400 lessons, had them work with the company’s engineers in a dedicated Slack group, and implemented improvements and security safeguards prior to the Teach mode launch. Still, to many who have seen the “move fast and break things” mantra of the tech industry play out, Lyu’s philosophy may sound concerning. In AI safety and responsibility circles in particular, there’s growing conversation about how companies should be seeking out every edge case internally before launch. And as my colleague Jeremy Kahn noted in Tuesday’s newsletter, some believe it’d be a good idea to slow the whole train. 

Who’s using the R1, anyway?

As Rabbit continues to work out its kinks, who’s using it? And for what? 

Teenagers, Lyu said, are currently the driving force of the product. On the flip side, he said they have elderly users who find just pressing the button easier than navigating apps on a smartphone. Additionally, it’s finding uses in specific industries: doctors who use it for translation when speaking with patients, and truck drivers who can’t use a smartphone while driving but can hit one button on the R1, similar to how they use the radio in their truck. 

While it’s easy to still see the R1 as cumbersome and unnecessary, these examples of how it’s being used show it may have some potential. I wouldn’t count out the R1 (well, a future version of it) just yet.
